Learning Objectives
Understand modern staging strategies and how they inform surgical planning.
Understand the role of soft-tissue reconstruction in patients with adult-acquired flatfoot
deformity.
Understand the role of osteotomies for deformity correction in patients with adult-acquired
flatfoot deformity.
Understand the role of arthrodesis in the management of adult-acquired flatfoot deformity.

The surgical management of adults with progressive collapse of the medial longitudinal
arch involves a broad discussion of the causes of the deformity and the various roles of
soft-tissue stabilization, realignment osteotomy, arthrodesis, and joint arthroplasty. The
management of this condition, although better understood than in years past, continues
to be a subject of debate. Recently a working group of experienced foot and ankle
surgeons published various recommendations. Although this constitutes level V expert
opinion, this Consensus Group drew on voluminous peer-reviewed literature.1
Terminology

Terminology
Adult-acquired flatfoot deformity (AAFD) has been the common descriptive term used to
describe the progression of a disease process most commonly derived from an
inflammatory and degenerative pathology of the posterior tibial tendon. Posterior tibial
tendon dysfunction also refers to this condition, emphasizing functional loss of the
tendon. Although these terms are commonly used, the Consensus Group has added the
term progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD).
Surgical Management Indications

Surgical Management Indications
In general, surgical management is indicated if reasonable attempts at nonsurgical
management fail to improve pain and associated disability. Other factors, such as
patient age, medical comorbidities, and desired activity level, must be considered in the
decision-making process.

Physical Examination
Body Mass Index

Body Mass Index
Patients with a body mass index higher than 30 kg/m2 generally have poorer outcomes
after reconstructive surgery than after hindfoot fusion. However, joint-sparing
procedures should be considered in younger patients.
Lower Extremity Alignment

Lower Extremity Alignment
The entire lower extremity should be examined with the patient standing and walking.
Knee deformity should be recognized if present. Asymmetry with the contralateral foot
may be appreciated.
Foot Alignment

Foot Alignment
Forefoot supination, midfoot collapse, and hindfoot valgus are common components of
AAFD. The location of the patient’s pain must be noted. Pain that is present more
medially over the posterior tibial tendon, over the midfoot, or at the sinus tarsi indicates
impingement, arthritis, or subfibular impingement.
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Adult-Acquired Flatfoot Deformity: Diagnosis and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000537
7/33

Gait

Gait
A shortened stride length, time in the stance phase, or external foot progression angle,
especially compared with the uninvolved side, may inform surgical decision making. Loss
of the medial longitudinal arch also will be visible during gait analysis, especially if
viewed from the side.
Gastrocnemius Contracture

Gastrocnemius Contracture
Achilles tendon contracture should be noted and the Silfverskiöld test to assess selective
gastrocnemius contracture should be performed because surgical lengthening may be
necessary to maintain postoperative deformity correction.
Stiffness/Reducibility of Deformity

Stiffness/Reducibility of Deformity
In addition to assessing the reducibility of the subtalar and talonavicular joints, a push-
up test can be performed to assess flexibility of forefoot varus. The patient is evaluated
on an examination table with the examiner seated. The assessment is performed by
positioning the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints in neutral alignment. The heel
should be in slight valgus, and the navicular should be centered on the talar head. Next,
dorsal-directed pressure is placed under the plantar first and fifth metatarsal heads to
dorsiflex the ankle to a neutral position. In a normal foot, the weight-bearing surface of
the calcaneus, the fifth metatarsal head, and the first metatarsal head should maintain a
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Adult-Acquired Flatfoot Deformity: Diagnosis and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000537
8/33

coplanar relationship. This is best visualized by observing down the weight-bearing plane
of the foot.
Heel/Toe Rise

Heel/Toe Rise
The posterior tibial tendon locks the transverse tarsal joint, allowing the heel to remain
in varus during heel rise. Patients with posterior tibial tendon dysfunction typically are
unable to perform a single-leg heel rise. Alternatively, patients may be able to perform a
single-leg heel rise but the heel remains in valgus. Having a patient perform a double-
limb heel rise typically will reveal hindfoot asymmetry, with the diseased limb remaining
in valgus (Figure 1).

Surgical Management
Goals

Goals
In the management of PCFD/AAFD, the combination of bone shape, soft-tissue failure,
and host factors must be considered. Realignment and balancing are the primary goals.
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Adult-Acquired Flatfoot Deformity: Diagnosis and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000537
10/33

Preservation of joint motion is preferred if possible; however, this must be balanced
against the need for fusion to attain and maintain correction.
Achilles/Gastrocnemius Lengthening

Achilles/Gastrocnemius Lengthening
Contracture of the triceps surae is a near-universal component of AAFD. As heel valgus
progresses and the Achilles tendon is transformed into a functional evertor of the
hindfoot, the triceps surae is relatively shortened. This is readily observed on passive
dorsiflexion of the ankle with the heel held in the corrected neutral position. In a normal
foot, dorsiflexion of the ankle 10° to 15° past neutral is possible with the hindfoot held in
neutral. Conversely, in a patient with AAFD, the ankle rarely can be dorsiflexed to
neutral, and attempts to do so result in obligate hindfoot valgus rather than true ankle
dorsiflexion. Because of this relationship, lengthening of part or all the heel cord has
become a standard component of most flatfoot reconstruction procedures; however,
which technique is most appropriate to accomplish this lengthening may be unclear.
Percutaneous Achilles tendon lengthening via the Hoke triple hemi-section technique is a
commonly used method for lengthening the Achilles tendon. This quick and simple
procedure involves three partial transverse tenotomies of the Achilles tendon, spaced at
2- to 4-cm intervals. Traditionally, in patients with valgus hindfoot deformity, two lateral
tenotomies are placed, one distal and one proximal, with a medial tenotomy between
them. After the tenotomies are performed, the ankle is gently dorsiflexed with the
hindfoot held in neutral. Under this gentle tension, the Achilles tendon lengthens
between the hemi-tenotomies, allowing an increase in passive ankle dorsiflexion. The
goal is to achieve easy dorsiflexion of the ankle to 10° to 15° past neutral with the
hindfoot held in a neutral position.
Alternately, equinus contracture associated with flatfoot can be addressed via
gastrocnemius recession. With this technique, lengthening is performed just distal to the
musculotendinous junction of the calf muscle. A posteromedial approach at the mid-calf
is used, and the sural nerve is identified and protected. If possible, the plane between
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Adult-Acquired Flatfoot Deformity: Diagnosis and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000537
11/33

the gastrocnemius and soleus tendons is developed just proximal to the point at which
they conjoin. Traditionally, the gastrocnemius fascia alone is released, after which the
ankle is passively dorsiflexed with the knee extended and a gap of 3 to 8 cm develops
between the cut ends of the gastrocnemius fascia. The amount of gap depends on the
severity of the contracture. Typically, this generates an additional 15° to 20° of ankle
dorsiflexion.
The strongest indication for gastrocnemius recession is a positive Silfverskiöld test
(Figure 2). This test primarily distinguishes between an isolated gastrocnemius
contracture or a combined gastrocnemius-soleus contracture. The latter also may
involve an ankle capsular contracture or anterior ankle impingement. The Silfverskiöld
test is performed by assessing passive ankle dorsiflexion with the hindfoot held in
neutral, first with the knee extended and then with the knee flexed. Improvement in
ankle dorsiflexion with the knee bent indicates the contracture is driven by isolated
tightness of the gastrocnemius muscle, which originates proximal to the knee.
Alternatively, lack of improvement in ankle dorsiflexion with knee flexion indicates a
combined gastrocnemius-soleus contracture, possibly in combination with a posterior
ankle capsular contracture.
Figure 2 Clinical photographs show the Silfverskiöld test. A, Incorrect method of
positioning the foot for examination. B, Correct technique, with the foot inverted to lock

the transverse tarsal joint. C, Dorsiflexion with the knee in extension. D, Dorsiflexion
with the knee in flexion. (Reproduced from Bohay DR, Anderson JG, Cheney NA, Rusk CL:
Metatarsal osteotomy to manage metatarsal prominence, in Alexander IJ, Bluman EM,
Greisberg JK, eds: Advanced Reconstruction: Foot and Ankle, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2015, pp 47-54.)
A relative indication for gastrocnemius recession is a younger, more active patient with
AAFD. Although percutaneous Achilles tendon lengthening is faster and easier to
perform, weakness caused by overlengthening is a concern. In practice, the amount of
lengthening that occurs with percutaneous Achilles tendon lengthening may be difficult
to control, and relative overlengthening is not uncommon. In older, lower demand
patients, this relative weakening of the triceps surae is well tolerated, and the patients
rarely are symptomatic. In younger, more active patients, persistent calf weakness may
be symptomatic. Such patients often demonstrate calf atrophy after surgical treatment.
As a result of these observations, the author of this lesson performs gastrocnemius
recession as part of flatfoot reconstruction in more active patients, even in the absence
of a positive Silfverskiöld test. If additional lengthening is required after the
gastrocnemius fascia has been released, the soleus fascia can be fractionally lengthened
via multiple small incisions to allow for additional dorsiflexion. This technique has not
resulted in overlengthening and facilitates earlier recuperation of strength and return to
athletic activity.
Occasionally, other procedures for releasing triceps surae contractures are necessary.
Vulpius lengthening or proximal gastrocnemius release can be performed if the
integument does not allow for safe lengthening more distally. Formal open Z-
lengthening may be required if the contracture prevents the patient from achieving 15°
of neutral ankle flexion.
Tenosynovectomy

Tenosynovectomy
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Adult-Acquired Flatfoot Deformity: Diagnosis and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000537
13/33

Open tenosynovectomy may be appropriate for stage I disease refractory to nonsurgical
management. This more often occurs in younger, athletic patients. Isolated
tenosynovectomy of the posterior tibial tendon should be performed only if no
substantial foot deformity is present. Endoscopic tenosynovectomy has been described
(Video 1). Note that isolated tenosynovectomy should be performed only in patients with
stage I disease, (tenosynovitis of the tendon without a length deficit) and no foot
deformity. Any deformity of the foot is associated with stage II disease.
Video 1 Mosca VS, Sangeorzan A, Sangeorzan BJ: The Flatfoot: Pediatric and Adult
Management [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021.
https://www.aaos.org/videos/video-detail-page/23082__Videos. Accessed March 18,
2021.
Tendon Transfer

Tendon Transfer
Wapner et al3 demonstrated that the flexor digitorum longus (FDL) is appropriate for
reconstruction in patients with posterior tibial tendon insufficiency because it is in-phase
with the posterior tibial tendon and also is immediately adjacent to it. Rosenfeld et al4
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Adult-Acquired Flatfoot Deformity: Diagnosis and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000537
14/33

demonstrated muscle hypertrophy on the MRIs of patients who underwent transfer of
the FDL tendon and substantially improved functional scores postoperatively.
Evaluation of the posterior tibial muscle belly is important in performing this transfer. In
patients with long-standing disease, the posterior tibial muscle becomes inelastic and
fails to contract if touched with electrocautery and loses its normal color. In such
patients, supplementation of the FDL tendon with the remnant of the posterior tibial
tendon is not advised; however, if the muscle appears normal, resection of the entire
diseased segment of the posterior tibial muscle and side-to-side transfer with the use of
a Pulvertaft weave of the FDL and posterior tibial tendons are recommended. If the
posterior tibial tendon itself is of poor-quality tissue or severely degenerated, it is
excised during this procedure because its retention would act as a pain generator.
Ligament Reconstruction
General Indications

General Indications
Evidence supports medial soft-tissue reconstruction, such as spring and deltoid ligament
reconstruction, for the management of severe PCFD/AAFD. The Consensus Group
recommends that spring ligament reconstruction be considered in addition to lateral
column lengthening (LCL) or subtalar fusion at the initial surgical procedure because
those procedures are associated with at least 50% correction but inadequate correction
of severe flexible subluxation of the talonavicular and subtalar joints. The Consensus
Group also recommends combined flatfoot reconstruction and deltoid reconstruction be
considered as a joint-sparing alternative in patients who have PCFD/AAFD with valgus
deformity of the ankle joint if 50% or more of the lateral joint space is remaining.
Spring Ligament
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Adult-Acquired Flatfoot Deformity: Diagnosis and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000537
15/33


Spring Ligament
In many patients with stage II AAFD, substantial deformity remains at the talonavicular
joint after calcaneal osteotomy and tendon transfer. Theoretically, support for and
correction of talonavicular deformity can be achieved via repair of a torn or attenuated
spring ligament in combination with passing the transferred tendon through the
navicular. However, in practice, this is not always the case. Spring ligament
reconstruction should be considered in patients with residual medial arch collapse,
critical attenuation of the spring ligament, and considerable talonavicular uncoverage
that cannot be corrected via an osteotomy. Various techniques have been described for
reconstruction of the spring ligament. Some techniques involve the use of allograft
tendon and other techniques involve the use synthetic suture suspensions. No
techniques are associated with long-term validated success. Therefore, in patients with
marked spring ligament disruption, a LCL procedure is added to reduce tension on this
repair (by improving talonavicular coverage).
Deltoid Ligament

Deltoid Ligament
Chronic deltoid insufficiency may occur in patients with long-standing PCFD/AAFD.
Combined reconstruction techniques with the spring ligament have been described.
Frequently, this incompetence occurs in combination with lateral ankle arthritis and is
appropriately managed via total ankle arthroplasty.
Osteotomy
General Considerations

General Considerations
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Adult-Acquired Flatfoot Deformity: Diagnosis and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000537
16/33

Calcaneal osteotomy has long been recognized as an important component of the
surgical management of flexible AAFD. The two most commonly performed calcaneal
osteotomies are a medial displacement calcaneal osteotomy (MDCO) of the calcaneal
tuberosity and LCL, which is an opening wedge osteotomy of the anterior portion of the
bone. MCDO and LCL often are performed simultaneously in patients with advanced
deformity. Finally, a dorsal opening wedge osteotomy of the medial cuneiform (Cotton
osteotomy) often is performed to manage residual dorsiflexion/supination of the medial
column.
Medial Displacement Calcaneal Osteotomy

Medial Displacement Calcaneal Osteotomy
An MDCO is effective for correcting hindfoot valgus. This restores the normal vector of
the Achilles tendon medial to the midline of the leg, allowing it to invert rather than evert
the hindfoot. An MDCO also protects the transferred FDL tendon. A major disadvantage
of an MDCO is its limited ability to reestablish talar head coverage. Therefore, an isolated
MDCO is strongly indicated in patients with mild to moderate flexible flatfoot deformity
characterized primarily by hindfoot valgus (stage IIA AAFD). This procedure also is
particularly amenable to minimally invasive surgical technique.
The case of a 65-year-old woman with posterior tibial tendon dysfunction and a flexible
AAFD corrected via MDCO and soft tissue reconstruction is shown in Figures 3, 4, 5 and

Calcaneal LCL

Calcaneal LCL
AAFD is a complex deformity with varying degrees of hindfoot valgus, forefoot
abduction, and midfoot supination. Although an MDCO can correct heel valgus,
it has far less ability to correct forefoot abduction. More severe forefoot
9/3/26, 7:15 AM
AAOS | Adult-Acquired Flatfoot Deformity: Diagnosis and Management
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000537
21/33

abduction, characterized by greater than 40% talonavicular uncoverage
observed on an AP foot radiograph, can be more effectively corrected via an LCL
procedure. Typical lengthening is 5 to 10 mm. Care must be taken to not
overcorrect the deformity, which may result in talonavicular adduction,
restricted subtalar eversion, and lateral column overload.
The procedure typically is performed through the anterior calcaneus,
approximately 1.2 to 1.5 cm proximal to the calcaneocuboid joint. Theoretically,
the osteotomy ideally traverses between the anterior and middle facets of the
subtalar joint. In practice, this is difficult to confirm. After the osteotomy is
completed, a lamina spreader or Kirschner wire distractor is used to open the
osteotomy. The more robust plantar soft tissues, including the lateral band of
the plantar fascia, tend to produce a bi-trapezoidal gap at the osteotomy site
that is widest dorsally and laterally. The gap is filled with contoured tricortical
allograft or autograft. Often, the graft is stable because of the inherent
compression present after the spreader is removed; however, internal fixation
usually is applied in the form of a percutaneous Kirschner wire, distal-to-
proximal screw, or lateral plate.
Although the exact mechanism by which the osteotomy corrects AAFD is not
completely understood, the technique can produce substantial improvement in
radiographic and clinical alignment. With this greater corrective power comes a
greater potential for complications. The most common complications are lateral
midfoot pain, nonunion, symptomatic hardware, subluxation of the
calcaneocuboid joint, and overcorrection. Given these potential complications,
LCL is most appropriately reserved for patients with more advanced deformity.
Relative contraindications include age older than 60 years and smoking, both of
which may be associated with an increased risk of nonunion.

Midfoot Stabilization for Residual Forefoot Supination

Midfoot Stabilization for Residual Forefoot Supination
The relationship between the hindfoot and forefoot must be considered. With
compromise of the static and dynamic stabilizers of the medial longitudinal
arch, compensatory forefoot varus (supination) occurs as the forefoot adapts to
chronic heel valgus. Less commonly, primary loss of the medial column
capsuloligamentous stabilizers may lead to progressive hindfoot deformity. In
both situations, the position of the forefoot may be addressed to reestablish the
coplanar tripod relationship of the calcaneus, the fifth metatarsal head, and the
first metatarsal head.
In patients with mild deformities and deformities of relatively short duration,
compensatory forefoot supination often is negligible or completely flexible.
Conversely, moderate to severe flatfoot may be associated with more advanced
and rigid forefoot supination. Left uncorrected, this elevation of the medial
column precludes reestablishment of a plantigrade foot. This may cause lateral
overload or gradual loss of correction and recurrence of deformity.
Substantial forefoot supination that persists despite hindfoot correction
typically is managed via a Cotton osteotomy (unless collapse is present at the
first tarsometarsal joint). This involves an opening wedge osteotomy of the
medial cuneiform. A vertical, transverse osteotomy of the medial cuneiform is
made through a dorsal incision, leaving the plantar cortex intact. A lamina
spreader or pin spreader is used to open the osteotomy, effectively plantar
flexing the first ray. The osteotomy is opened until the first metatarsal head is
coplanar with the fifth metatarsal head and calcaneus. An appropriately sized
triangular graft is then inserted to fill the osteotomy, and internal fixation is

osteotomy is quite stable and heals reliably with little morbidity; however,
because it usually is performed distal to the apex of deformity and because it
does not de-rotate the entire forefoot, it is best suited for patients with mild to
moderate deformity. It also is contraindicated in patients with considerable
arthritis. Therefore, if instability or arthritis of the medial column is present,
then arthrodesis of the involved joint may be necessary. This procedure
essentially creates more of a cavus foot deformity at the medial column of the
foot. Therefore, surgeons must ensure that lateral column overload does not
occur at the fifth metatarsal base as a result of medial column restoration of
height.
Talonavicular arthrodesis is indicated for the correction of forefoot varus in
patients with severe varus and abduction and in patients in whom arthritic
changes and the apex of deformity are localized to this joint. Usually, this is
accomplished as part of double or triple hindfoot arthrodesis. Frequently, the
talonavicular joint is without arthritic changes and the apex of deformity lies at
the naviculocuneiform joint, particularly in patients with a flexible, stage II
flatfoot deformity. In this situation, the decision is between naviculocuneiform
fusion and a Cotton osteotomy. Although substantial, painful arthritis is the
strongest indication for naviculocuneiform fusion to correct forefoot varus, even
in the absence of arthritis, this fusion is a particularly effective technique.
Because the naviculocuneiform articulation often is the apex of the deformity,
fusion at that articulation represents a powerful corrective procedure. The
procedure can be performed via a medial approach, in which only the medial
and middle naviculocuneiform articulations are fused, or via a dorsal approach
to allow for fusion of all three naviculocuneiform joints. In both situations, the
corrective maneuver involves de-rotating and slightly plantar flexing the
supinated forefoot. If the foot is rigid and cannot be de-rotated sufficiently, a
cuboid osteotomy is performed to ensure rotational correction.
Fixation is accomplished with the use of a combination of lag screws and small
plates. In general, bone grafting is recommended. Naviculocuneiform fusion is
an excellent treatment option for patients with arthritis, instability, or marked

Peritalar subluxation represents an important component of PCFD and, with progression, may
result in arthritic changes and rigid deformity. In these situations, arthrodesis may be

Triple Arthrodesis

Triple Arthrodesis
Fusion of all three joints of the hindfoot is a powerful surgical procedure for the
correction of stiff, uncorrectable stage III flatfoot deformity. This comprehensive
procedure addresses each element of the AAFD. Subtalar fusion corrects hindfoot
valgus, restoring calcaneal pitch and eliminating subfibular impingement. Transverse
tarsal fusion corrects forefoot abduction and compensatory forefoot varus (thereby
reestablishing the weight-bearing tripod of the foot) and may accentuate the longitudinal
arch. Another important advantage of this approach is that any concomitant arthritic
changes in the hindfoot joints are addressed.
This comprehensive correction procedure is not without potential sequelae. Hindfoot
motion is eliminated after successful triple arthrodesis. This loss of motion increases
stress on the adjacent joints, including the ankle, predisposing these joints to
subsequent instability and arthritis. In addition, each joint represents a site of potential
nonunion. Because of these concerns, selective or partial hindfoot arthrodesis has
emerged as an alternative to triple arthrodesis.
Partial Hindfoot Arthrodesis

Partial Hindfoot Arthrodesis
Acceptable examples of selective hindfoot fusion for AAFD include isolated subtalar
fusion with FDL tendon transfer, isolated talonavicular fusion, transverse tarsal fusion,
and double fusion consisting of subtalar plus talonavicular fusion with preservation of
the calcaneocuboid joint.

Although subtalar fusion allows for repositioning and stabilization of the talus on top of
the calcaneus, it may not fully correct advanced forefoot abduction and does not correct
forefoot varus. Such varus may be addressed via talonavicular fusion or, for more distal
deformity, naviculocuneiform fusion. The naviculocuneiform joint has a curvature in the
sagittal plane. Therefore, preservation of the shape of the joint is the key to permitting
plantar flexion correction by rotating the midfoot along the débrided joint surfaces.
Talonavicular fusion also should be considered in patients with talonavicular arthritis or
sag and patients in whom adequate correction of talonavicular abduction deformity
cannot be achieved intraoperatively.

arthrodesis in lieu of triple fusion, even in patients with severe, long-standing deformity,
with good results. The case of a 78-year-old woman with fixed late-stage AAFD is shown

Stage IV deformity is characterized by a rigid flatfoot in combination with valgus of the
tibiotalar joint. Ankle valgus results from progression of the same pathophysiologic
forces that produce hindfoot valgus and arch collapse. As the severity of hindfoot valgus
increases, the mechanical axis of the leg moves progressively more medial with respect
to the foot, producing increased stress on the medial stabilizers of the ankle, particularly
the deltoid. As the deltoid attenuates under persistent increased valgus stress, the talus
begins to tilt into valgus within the ankle mortise. Such valgus exacerbates subfibular
impingement and increases contact stresses in the lateral tibiotalar joint, eventually
resulting in ankle arthritis. Most patients with stage IV flatfoot also have a rigid hindfoot
valgus deformity; however, ankle valgus also may occasionally be observed in
combination with flexible hindfoot deformities.
Treatment options for stage IV flatfoot include bracing, bracing after hindfoot
realignment, pantalar fusion, or hindfoot realignment with deltoid ligament
reconstruction. In 2007, stage IV was further subclassified based on these factors. Stage
IVA deformity is characterized by valgus tilt of the talus that is correctable and without
arthritic changes. Stage IVB deformity describes ankle valgus that is no longer
correctable and/or demonstrates substantial arthritic changes. Surgical decision making
is guided by whether the talus is correctable within the mortise and by the severity of
arthritic changes.
Hindfoot Reconstruction

Hindfoot Reconstruction
Joint-preserving reconstruction can be attempted in patients with a stage IVA valgus
ankle. For mild ankle valgus (0° to 3°), aggressive hindfoot realignment alone may be
adequate if it adequately medializes the mechanical axis of the leg. Postoperative use of
an articulated ankle-foot orthosis should be considered in these patients.

Hindfoot Realignment and Deltoid Reconstruction

Hindfoot Realignment and Deltoid Reconstruction
If valgus tilt is more substantial (4° to 10°) but the joint is reducible, preservation of the
ankle via deltoid ligament reconstruction in combination with hindfoot realignment is
recommended. The goal is to restore and stabilize the talus in its normal position within
the ankle mortise. Research to determine the best deltoid ligament reconstruction
technique is ongoing; however, the most promising techniques involve the use of
allograft tendon to reconstruct the superficial and the deep portions of the deltoid
ligament. Regardless of technique, deltoid ligament reconstruction appears to result in
the best outcomes in patients with valgus tilt of <10°; recurrence of tilt is common in
patients with greater deformity (Figures 9 and 10).

Total Ankle Arthroplasty

Total Ankle Arthroplasty
Total ankle arthroplasty may be performed in combination with or after hindfoot
reconstruction or fusion in patients who have AAFD associated with ankle valgus. Ankle
arthroplasty is associated with the potential for preservation of tibiotalar motion but
possibly with a greater risk for failure in patients with deltoid insufficiency. Therefore,
additional research is being performed in patients with stage IV flatfoot deformity; many
hope that the findings of such research will aid in refining the surgical decision-making
process for patients with stage IV flatfoot deformity (Figure 11).

Extended Ankle Fusion

Extended Ankle Fusion
Pantalar fusion will address the arthritis and deformity associated with rigid stage IV
disease. These procedures can produce a stable, plantigrade foot with less pain;
however, loss of motion and function may pose a considerable challenge for patients.
